source.title: When Trees Are Not Enough: Learning Mixed-Topology Feature Graphs with Adaptive Graph Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Xiao-Zuo Shen; Yi-Fei Cai; Tian Tan; Rui Ning; Chun-Sheng Xin; Hong-Yi Wu

page_placements.theme: Absorption depends on the SAE objective and architecture, not only on size or sparsity

record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures feature absorption and reports that a graph-guided realignment update reduces it, refining the absorption-related challenge in V4.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions feature splitting as prior work but does not itself test splitting across SAE sizes, input partitioning, or directional proximity. Its own relevant result is an absorption evaluation before and after realignment. Causal-intervention results do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper (AG-SAE). Its only results bearing on a claim version are absorption rates under the SAEBench first-letter protocol for conventional SAEs on Gemma-2-2B layer 13. These are the Abs. column of Table 1D and the pre-realignment baseline in Fig. 7. They show absorption arising in standard BatchTopK SAEs in a new setting. It does not vary dictionary size or sparsity, and it does not test splitting itself.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is too narrow. The authors' main conclusion is that AG-SAE learns reliable mixed-topology (zero-, single- and multi-parent) feature graphs. These graphs beat structured and post-hoc baselines on predictive, non-redundancy and semantic validity, and AG-SAE features give stronger causal interventions. A secondary result is that Absorption Realignment reduces absorption with EV and L0 nearly unchanged, so recovered structure can guide dictionary refinement.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses complete parent-set graph induction and graph-guided dictionary refinement, rather than testing the size-scaling feature-splitting procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: A single graph-guided Absorption Realignment update on a fixed trained SAE lowers absorption fraction from 42.08% to 28.11% and full absorption from 38.92% to 27.56%. EV and L0 are essentially unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Absorption in trained SAEs can be partly corrected post hoc by reallocating parent-aligned decoder content, without reconstruction or sparsity cost.

fits_no_version.finding: In AG-SAE graphs over four dictionary widths, 23.55% of parented features have multiple parents. Roots concentrate in narrow banks (27.29% at 2,048) and leaves in wide banks (18.85% at 16,384). Depth reaches 8 edges, beyond the scale hierarchy. The pattern replicates on PubMed and Qwen3.5-2B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relations among SAE features across dictionary scales form a mixed-topology DAG rather than single-parent trees. Coarse features sit in narrow dictionaries and refinements in wide ones.

record.problems: The absorption result is from a targeted evaluation on one fixed SAE with one realignment update; the paper does not report uncertainty for these absorption measurements or test changes in dictionary size or sparsity.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant splitting results were reported. Causal-intervention results were left out because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No comparison of a coarse feature with its finer replacements across dictionary sizes, and no measure of input coverage or directional proximity of split features.
No test of splitting in large models or open SAE releases. Cross-model results (Qwen3.5-2B, PubMed) concern AG-SAE graph topology.
No test that split features form nested, geometrically close families mirroring a concept hierarchy in conventional SAEs.
No variation of SAE size or sparsity to test whether absorption persists. Parent-off/child-on is only measured via the benchmark aggregate.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents and no count of novel latents.
No test attributing splitting to the sparsity objective. Matryoshka is compared only on absorption, reconstruction and relation reliability, not on splitting.

missing.what: Absorption score by method at matched L0≈50: Vanilla 51.39, Matryoshka 12.71, HSAE 10.24, Tree SAE 5.11 (at lower L0 40.84), AG-SAE 9.16. Conventional SAEs absorb heavily, while alternative objectives reduce but do not eliminate absorption.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not among the original sources. Absorption numbers differ between Table 1D (Vanilla 51.39) and the realignment experiment (42.08). They likely come from different SAEs or cohorts, and the paper does not reconcile them. No uncertainty is given for any absorption measure. The realignment result is a mitigation and does not bear on V4's clause that size/sparsity changes don't fix absorption. For that reason it gets no limits_scope label. The Matryoshka absorption reduction is only reported as a baseline comparison.

versions.untested_parts: No measurement of a coarse feature being replaced by finer features as dictionary size grows, their input coverage, or their directional proximity.
Cross-model and cross-domain results concern learned mixed-topology graphs, not the claimed size-related feature-splitting pattern or open SAE releases.
The study does not test whether split features are nested, geometrically close families that mirror a concept hierarchy.
It measures absorption before and after realignment, but does not directly test parent inactivity where a child activates, or vary SAE size or sparsity.
No comparison showing larger-SAE latents as combinations of smaller-SAE latents or measuring novel latents against canonicality.
No test attributing splitting to the sparsity objective or comparing objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs for splitting.

rows.subject: fixed, fully trained SAE
rows.operation_detail: Apply one Absorption Realignment update using the graph from Complete Parent-Set Induction.
rows.note: The update reduces but does not eliminate measured absorption.
rows.check: The row compares the study's own realignment update against its pre-update baseline, so the 'value' is method performance. Only the baseline (42.08% absorption fraction in a conventionally trained SAE) bears on V4, and it shows absorption present. The subject is not identified beyond 'fixed, fully trained SAE', presumably the Gemma-2-2B layer-13 BatchTopK SAE. The reduction to 28.11% is a mitigation result, not a test of V4.
